prime.problem: cuBLAS is fast but closed: you can't fuse your own activation into its output, so a custom epilogue costs an extra kernel and a round trip of C through HBM. A block-level matmul you can edit needs to match cuBLAS without siboehm's ten kernels, and its speed turns out to depend on something the math never mentions: which tiles run at the same time.
prime.fits: It combines the Triton programming model with the matmul cards: the same block tiling siboehm wrote by hand, with the thread-level work left to the compiler. It adds L2-aware launch order and autotuning, and points to FlashAttention's Triton kernel in perf-4.
expect: one program per C tile, a K loop with tl.dot
grouped (super-grouped) launch order and L2 reuse
prime.goal: Write the tutorial's matmul structure from memory, count the distinct blocks a set of concurrent programs touches under any grouping, and say when grouping and autotuning pay off.

attend: What does the program no longer write that siboehm's kernels spelled out by hand?
Why does the accumulator stay fp32 when the inputs are fp16, and where does the result get rounded?
Every tile of C is computed whatever the launch order. So how can order change speed?
Why does GROUP_SIZE_M = 8 do nothing for the tutorial's 9 concurrent programs, yet cut distinct blocks 2.62× for a T4-sized wave?
What does the autotuner re-run when the shape changes, and why does a T4 search a much smaller space than an A100?

must: Each program owns one BM × BN tile of C and walks K, loading one block of A and one of B per step and accumulating with tl.dot in fp32 → the compiler picks warp and thread tiles, shared-memory staging, vector loads and the tensor-core instruction → 29 lines reach 99% of cuBLAS at 4096² on the tutorial's GPU

Only programs running at the same moment share L2 → row-major order makes a wave sweep a long row of C, pulling in every B strip → grouping GROUP_SIZE_M rows at a time makes the wave a compact block → distinct blocks fall (90 → 54 in the 9 × 9 example) → more L2 hits, fewer HBM reads

Distinct blocks = K_b × (rows + columns covered) → smallest when the wave's footprint is square (g ≈ √W) → grouping helps only when the wave spans enough tiles; with one row of tiles (decode) or a tiny wave, every order is the same

Tile shape trades reuse (BM·BN/(BM + BN) FLOP/B per tile) against parallelism and shared memory → the best config differs by shape and GPU → @triton.autotune times a config list the first time it sees each (M, N, K) and caches the winner
elevated: A single 128 × 256 tile streaming from HBM sits at 85 FLOP/B, far under the H100's 295 ridge → the GEMM is compute-bound only because concurrent programs reuse blocks through L2 → launch order is what sets that reuse (294 FLOP/B row-major vs 805 grouped in the Llama up-projection model)
reference: the 16 tutorial configs and the fp8 note on BK = 128
unit-test tolerances (atol 1e-2, fp8 0.125) and the 31-size benchmark table

compress.prompt: From memory, sketch the 9 × 9 grid of C tiles and shade the first 9 programs under row-major and under GROUP_SIZE_M = 3. Count the A and B strips each touches and write the block totals. Then add one line for what autotuning chooses and one for what it can't.
checklist: row-major: 1 A strip + 9 B strips = 10 strips × 9 blocks = 90
the order doesn't change total work, only which blocks can be L2 hits
autotune picks block sizes, K width, stages and warps per shape, by timing
it can't pick what isn't in the config list, and configs that exceed the GPU's shared memory fail to compile and are skipped

retrieve.q: Explain why launch order changes a matmul's speed even though every program does the same work in any order.
answer: neighbouring tiles share input strips (same row of A, same column of B)
L2 only helps if the programs needing a block run while it's still cached
the order decides which programs run together, so it sets how many blocks come from L2 instead of HBM

retrieve.q: Using the tutorial's mapping, count distinct blocks for the first 9 programs on a 9 × 9 grid (K_b = 9) with GROUP_SIZE_M = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 9.
When is grouped ordering not worth the six lines, and what would you try instead where it does matter a lot?
answer: decode with ≤ 128 tokens and BM = 128: one row of tiles, every order identical
small matrices whose A and B fit in L2 anyway (1024² fp16 on an H100)
when L2 hit rate is already high (siboehm's ~80%, no gain)
where it matters: persistent kernels that walk tiles in a chosen order, or Hilbert-curve ordering (Shankhdhar's H100 worklog)

compare.q: siboehm's thread swizzling gave nothing on an A6000; Triton's grouping gave 1.11× on an A100. Name the differences in setup that could explain it, and what the card says you can and can't conclude.
answer: different GPU, matrix sizes, precision (FP32 vs fp16) and compute unit (CUDA cores vs tensor cores)
siboehm's L2 hit rate was already ~80%
neither source explains the gap, so the only honest conclusion is to measure on your shape and GPU

compare.q: Tutorial 06's fused attention uses the same program-per-tile pattern as this matmul. What does each program own and loop over in each kernel, and what extra state must the attention program carry across its loop?
answer: matmul: one C tile, looping over K blocks of A and B
attention: one block of queries, looping over K/V blocks
attention also carries a running max and sum for the softmax, rescaling the accumulator as each block arrives

predict.q: Decode with 64 tokens through the Llama up-projection (M = 64, K = 4,096, N = 14,336) using the tutorial's first config (BM = 128, BN = 256). Commit: how many tiles, how many rows of tiles, and does GROUP_SIZE_M change anything?
predict.answer: M = 64 fits in one 128-row tile (half of it masked), so there is one row of tiles: 14,336 ÷ 256 = 56 tiles in total. With one row, the grouped mapping gives exactly the row-major order, so GROUP_SIZE_M changes nothing. On an H100 those 56 programs don't even fill the 132 SMs; smaller tiles or split-K would, and the kernel is memory-bound on the weights anyway.

Then add a row for W = 64 concurrent programs on the 32 × 32 tile grid (K_b = 32): predict the best g from √W before running, and compare its block count with row-major. Finally, estimate shared memory per config as stages × (BM·BK + BK·BN) × 2 B for four of the tutorial's configs and mark which fit a T4's 64 KB.
apply.done: You predicted the best g for W = 64 before running and can say whether g = 8 beat row-major and by how much; your shared-memory estimates give 144 KB for 128 × 256 × 64 × 3 stages and exactly 64 KB for 128 × 128 × 32 × 4.
apply.hint: √64 = 8, so expect g = 8 to be near-best. Row-major with W = 64 on a 32-column grid covers 2 rows and all 32 columns.
